{{nihongo|'''Ōi Shrine'''|大井神社|Ōi-jinja}} is a Shinto shrine in {{ill|Mito, Ibaraki|en|Mito, Ibaraki|qid=Q204249|lt=Mito, Ibaraki}}, {{ill|Ibaraki Prefecture|en|Ibaraki Prefecture|qid=Q83273|lt=Ibaraki Prefecture}}. It is listed as a {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|ja|延喜式神名帳|zh|延喜式神名帳|simple|Engishiki Jinmyocho|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle|lt=Shikinai}} {{ill|Engishiki_Jinmyōchō#Ronsha|de|Ronsya|ja|論社|2=ja|3=論社|lt=candidate|zh|论社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ronsya|13=User:Immanuelle/candidate shrines|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki_Jinmyocho|lt=Ronsha}}, with its modern shrine ranking as a former {{ill|Son-sha|de|Dorfschrein|ja|村社|qid=Q134917284}}{{efn|Former shrine rank|lt=Son-sha|1=modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|zh|村社|1=Son-sha|WD=Q134917284}}{{efn|Former shrine rank|lt=Son-sha|1=Modern_system_of_ranked_Shinto_shrines#Village_shrines|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/village shrine|qq=ja_comment|qid=Q134917284|qq= 近代社格制度|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q712534}}.

== Worshipped deities ==
{{see also|{{ill|Saijin|de|Saijin|ja|祭神|zh|祭神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saijin|qq=}}}}
'''Primary deity'''
* {{ill|Takekashima-no-Mikoto|de|Takekashima-no-Mikoto|ja|建借馬命|zh|建借马命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takekashima-no-Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} — the first head of the Nakakuni-no-Miyatsuko.

'''Secondary deity'''
* {{ill|Konohanasakuya-hime|de|Konohanasakuya-hime|ja|木花開耶姫命|zh|木花开耶姬命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Konohanasakuya-hime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to QID FIXED|qid=Q1781862}} — enshrined by amalgamation of a subordinate shrine.

=== About the primary deity ===
According to the *Kuni-no-Miyatsuko Honki* (volume 10 of the *Sendai Kuji Hongi*), Takekashima-no-Mikoto shares ancestry with the Iyo no Kuni-no-Miyatsuko and was appointed the first Nakakuni-no-Miyatsuko during Emperor Seimu’s reign<ref>『国造本紀』仲国造条。</ref>. The *Hitachi-no-Kuni Fudoki* records him (as “Takekashima-no-Mikoto”) subduing eastern rebels under Emperor Sujin<ref>『常陸国風土記』行方郡条。</ref>.  

Remains linked to him include the Atago-yama Kofun (Atagoyama tumulus) in Atago-chō, Mito (traditionally his grave)<ref>[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/… 愛宕山古墳] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education).</ref><ref name="explain"/>. The shrine’s name “Ōi” and the place name “Iitomi” are also said to derive from his descendant Ōfu-no-Omi, descended from Kamu-Yai-Mimi-no-Mikoto<ref name="explain"/>.

In *Jinmyōchō Kōshō*, degree of freedom names him as Kamu-Yai-Mimi-no-Mikoto. Some traditions link “Kashima” in his name to enshrinement by the Kasuga (Kashima) and Katori shrines.

== History ==
=== Origins ===
Shrine tradition holds that on Emperor Sujin’s order, Prince Toyokiiri-hiko-no-Mikoto brought Takekashima-no-Mikoto here and enshrined Amaterasu-Ōmikami on a nearby hill<ref name="explain"/>.

In the Nara period, the ujibe clan of Naka District worshipped Takekashima-no-Mikoto<ref name="explain"/>.

=== Overview ===
In the mid-Heian period, the *Engishiki Jinja-myochō* lists it as “Ōi Shrine of Naka District, Hitachi Province,” ranking it among the *Shikinaisha*<ref> [http://www.ibaraki-jinjacho.jp/… 大井神社] (Ibaraki Shrine Office).</ref>. However, a decree of junior fifth rank from 845 AD likely refers to another Ōi Shrine in Suruga Province. The Ōi Shrine in Kasama is also a *Ronsya*.  

In the late Muromachi period, the shrine burned; it was rebuilt in Eishō (1504–1521) but again damaged by fire in 1588. In 1668, Tokugawa Mitsukuni ordered repairs, naming it “Katori Daimyōjin,” but it reverted to Ōi Shrine during Kansei (1789–1801). The current haiden dates to Ansei (1854–1859). In the Meiji era it was designated a village shrine under the modern ranking system.
